title: Erect a trellis system for the growing of vines

lessons.title: Trellis parts and materials
lessons.html:
Trellis parts and materials

A vine cannot stand up on its own. A trellis is a system of posts and wires that holds the vine up. It keeps the leaves open to the sun and air, keeps the grapes off the ground, and makes pruning, spraying and picking easier.

Common trellis systems in South Africa

  • Vertical shoot positioning (VSP): one cordon wire with movable foliage wires above it. Shoots are tucked upwards between the wires. Common for wine grapes.
  • Slanting or cross-arm trellis: a cross-piece on top of the post spreads the canopy wider. Used for some wine and table grape blocks.
  • Gable or pergola: used mostly for table grapes, with a high canopy that grapes hang under.

Your farm manager chooses the system. You must build it exactly as the plan says.

Parts of the trellis

  • End posts (anchor posts): thick, treated wooden posts at the end of each row. They carry the pull of all the wires.
  • Anchors: a buried anchor or stay that holds the end post so it does not lean inwards.
  • Line posts: thinner posts placed along the row at a fixed spacing.
  • Cordon wire: the strong wire that the vine's arms (cordons) are tied to.
  • Foliage (catch) wires: wires above the cordon that hold the shoots up.
  • Drip line wire: a low wire for the irrigation pipe on some farms.
  • Stakes: a thin stake at each vine to guide the young vine straight up to the cordon wire.

Tools

Fencing pliers, wire strainer, wire cutters, tape measure, string line, spade, post-hole digger or tractor post driver, and a crowbar.

lessons.title: Building the trellis safely
lessons.html:
Building the trellis safely

Steps

  1. Mark the rows. Use the vineyard plan, a tape measure and pegs. Rows must be straight and evenly spaced so tractors can drive between them.
  2. Put in the end posts. Set them deep and leaning slightly outwards, away from the row. Ram the soil in hard, layer by layer.
  3. Fit the anchors. Bury the anchor outside the row and connect it to the top of the end post with strong wire. Tension it so the post is firm.
  4. Put in the line posts. Use a string line to keep them straight. Space them as the plan says. Make the tops level.
  5. Run out the wires. Roll the cordon wire along the row without kinks. Fix one end to the end post.
  6. Strain the wires. Use the wire strainer at the other end. Bring the wire to the tension your supervisor gives. Fix the wire to each line post at the correct height with staples or clips. Do the same for foliage wires.
  7. Put in the vine stakes next to each planting spot, straight and firm, and tie them to the cordon wire.

Checking your work

  • Rows are straight when you look along them.
  • End posts are firm and do not move when pushed.
  • Wires are at the same height all along the row.
  • Wire tension is correct: tight but not over-strained.

Safety

  • Wear leather gloves, safety glasses, boots and long sleeves.
  • Never stand in line with a wire being strained; it can snap and whip back.
  • Lift heavy end posts with two or more people.
  • Stay clear of the tractor post driver. Never put your hands near the hammer while it is working.
  • Do not touch treated wooden posts and then eat; wash your hands first.
  • Pick up all offcuts of wire.

Maintenance

Check the trellis each winter before pruning. Re-tension slack wires, fix broken wires and replace broken or rotten posts.

Key points

  • A trellis holds vines up and keeps the canopy open to sun and air.
  • End posts and anchors carry the pull of the wires.
  • Use a plan, pegs and a string line to keep rows straight.
  • Strain wires to the right tension and keep them at the same height.
  • Never stand in line with a wire under strain.
